lastCommit.message:
OTA-1840 — the house keeps its key

Three faults on the pairing authority, one root: a cache that holds `null | T`
is one state short, and a row rebuilt from a field whitelist keeps only the
fields somebody remembered to list.

(A) KEY PRESERVATION. `loadPaired()` rebuilt each stored row as
{player, installId, addedTs} and never copied `key`, while `persistPaired()`
writes the whole row with JSON.stringify — so a sealed pairing's key reached
the disk intact and was discarded on the way back. This was worse than a lost
verification. With every key gone the install holds NO keys at all, and a
phone holding no keys is by design a phone from before seals existed: it
admits an unsealed payload. The restart turned a REFUSAL INTO AN ACCEPTANCE.
Measured pre-repair: a forged payload, refused before the restart, was
accepted after it (forged false, added 1).

(B) PAIRED LIST. `cachedPaired()` installed `[]` as the answer and
`loadPaired()` early-returns on a truthy PAIRED, so one synchronous look
before the disk answered left the install unpaired for the session. Measured:
an arriving corpse turned away as a stranger (added 0 of 1), and the next
write persisted the empty list over the real one (House A erased).

(C) HOUSE NAME. `cachedHouseName()` did the same with `''`; this install's
dead rode out to other players' rolls stamped "an unnamed house" while the
name sat on disk.

All three take OTA-1839's state model: `null` means unhydrated, a sync reader
gets a non-installing fallback (frozen UNHYDRATED_PAIRED / literal ''),
hydration is serialised behind one in-flight promise, and it installs only if
the cache is still `null` so a late read cannot clobber a mutation that landed
meanwhile. Row revival is factored into revivePairedRow, which CARRIES the
stored key — the trim and 64-char bound are exactly what parseHouseCode
already applied on the way in, so it is idempotent and cannot turn a real key
into a different one.

Security policy is untouched: no change to the HMAC, key derivation, seal
format, house-code format, trust classification, or the acceptance rules for
foreign payloads. No key is invented for a legacy keyless row — an old TAR1
card stays paired and unsealed, a keyless house is still admitted as unsealed
rather than silently authenticated, and an unpaired house is still refused.
No schema change, no migration; the on-disk format already carried the key.

New suite ota1840TheHouseKeepsItsKey: 26 tests, 14 red before the repair.
Three negative controls, one per defect, each red at the tests that name it
and restored hash-clean. Test 6.5 was rewritten during the work: it had taken
a 1400-char window after loadPaired and required the substring "key", which
PAIRED_KEY alone satisfies — it pinned nothing and would have passed on the
broken code. It now writes a key to disk by hand and demands it back byte for
byte.

Adjacent, reported not absorbed: cachedInstallId() still installs '', the same
shape. It is not a live defect ('' is falsy, so ensureInstallId still reaches
the disk), but two concurrent cold calls could in principle mint two ids.
Identity/trust, outside this task's scope.

Validation: focused 26/26; Fallen + seal + OTA-1838/1839 regressions 143/143;
typecheck 181 (pre-existing baseline, unchanged); 25/25 local gates; full fast
surface 1344/1344 suites, 15,248 passed / 3 skipped, no failures and no flakes.
